subject: A question about a simulation test with small sample size

messages.author: a29b76a7fee2ac43
messages.subject: A question about a simulation test with small sample size
parts:
Hello all,

I am planning to perform a simulation test to find out how many responses I need to collect so that the model RMSEA is less than a certain threshold. I have been reading articles here and there about monte carlo simulation, and I am not sure if I am on the right track. I would be grateful if someone can give me some advice/feedback about my steps here.

Basically, I collected some pilot data (n=15) from a questionnaire with 100 items (6 questions with 7 categories, and the rest with 5 categories). So, I most likely ended with a multidimensional gpcm. With such a small dataset, I did an exploratory factor analysis using Jamovi and it figures it is about three factors (skeptical, but I assume it is ok and ran with it).

So now, assuming that this is a 3-dimensional gpcm model, I use mirt to create a model with 15 responses and evaluate it using M2. Unsurprisingly, the RMSEA is 0.1993603. 

Now, assuming that the model is appropriate, I would like to find out how many samples I need to bring the RMSEA down below a certain threshold. So, I used simdata to generate data (using model = the_naive_model_with_15_samples), I tried 250, 500, and 1000 samples, I can see the RMSEA is coming down quite a lot (n=500 is 0.006, and n=1000 is 0.003, however with p-value > 0.1 though).

So my question is, is this an acceptable way to get a sense of how many responses I need to collect from the pilot data?

 Any comment would be much appreciated...thanks! 🙏

messages.author: b330c2028fed415b
messages.subject: Re: A question about a simulation test with small sample size
parts:
No idea what you mean by 'bringing the RMSEA down'. This statistic using M2() is a point estimate of how poorly a model fits the data in terms of first and second moments, and is influenced by a wide variety of factors (dimensionality, item-data fit, pattern of loadings, sample size, influential cases, etc). No doubt with such a small sample size the CI for the RMSEA is extremely wide, so the point estimate itself is a poor representation of how well the model fits the data. As you noted, in a perfect world RMSEA → 0 as N → ∞, so in that sense it will always be positive in any given sample, but I don't think it makes sense to look at this statistic as a function of sample size in isolation.

Phil
